title: Space & Territory
hook: People defend a chair, a desk or a side of the bed as if it were their skin, and the markers they leave tell you what they think they own.
why:
The chapter on proxemics described the bubble of space people carry around with them. This chapter is about something different: the places people claim and defend even when they are not standing in them. A regular seat at the pub. A desk in a shared office. A side of the bed. A chair at the family table that nobody else sits in. A parking space outside the house that is, legally, anyone's.

People feel these claims strongly, and they react to violations of them with an intensity that often surprises everyone involved, themselves included. The research on territory explains why, and it gives a reader a rich source of information. You will learn the kinds of territory and how they differ, how people mark their claims and how others respect the markers, what happens when territory is invaded, why people behave differently on their own ground, what rooms reveal about the people who use them, why losing territory can hurt far more than it seems it should, and how to read and respect the claims around you, including your own.

teach.h: Territory is space with a claim on it.
teach.p:
Personal space travels with you. Territory stays put. The social psychologist Irwin Altman, writing in 1975, distinguished three kinds of territory according to how strong and lasting the claim is.

Primary territories are owned and used exclusively and over long periods, and are central to a person's sense of who they are: a home, a bedroom, sometimes a car or a private office. Intrusion into them is felt as a serious violation. Secondary territories are used regularly and claimed informally, but not owned: a regular seat at the pub, a desk in a shared office, a particular table at the café, a bench in the park where the same group of friends always meets. The claim is real but negotiable, and disputes over secondary territories are common. Public territories are claimed only temporarily and only while in use: a table in a library, a spot on a beach, a seat on a train.

The kinds shade into one another. A family dinner table is a primary territory for the family, and each person's chair at it may be a small primary territory within it. A teenager's bedroom is often the first primary territory a young person can call their own, which is why its door matters so much.

For a reader, the useful question about any space is: whose is it, and how strongly? A man sitting in someone else's regular seat, a new colleague at a desk that used to be another's, a guest who settles into the host's armchair: each has stepped into a claim, and the people around will often react before anyone says a word.

Ask whose space it is before you read how people behave in it.
teach.disconfirm: If people reacted to the use of their regular seat, desk or chair no more strongly than to the use of any other seat, the idea of secondary territory would add nothing. Watch what happens the next time someone sits in a seat that is usually someone else's.

teach.p:
People leave objects behind to hold their claims: a coat on a chair, a towel on a sunbed, a bag on a library table, a mug on a desk, a jacket over the back of a seat in a meeting room. In the late 1960s and early 1970s Robert Sommer and Franklin Becker studied these markers in libraries and canteens.

Markers worked. Tables with personal belongings left on them were avoided by newcomers for much longer than empty tables, and the more personal the marker, a jacket rather than a stack of library magazines, the longer it held the space. Neighbours took part in the defence too. When a newcomer approached a marked seat, people sitting nearby would often tell them it was taken, defending a claim that was not theirs.

Markers are a language almost everyone understands without being taught. They also tell you something about how people see their place. The colleague who covers a hot desk with photographs, a plant and a personal mug every morning is claiming more than a work surface. The guest who leaves their bag by the door rather than unpacking is keeping a light claim. The partner who keeps a toothbrush at your flat but no clothes has marked a particular level of belonging.

Changes in marking are worth noticing. A person who stops personalising their desk, clears away their photographs or leaves their coat on rather than hanging it up may be loosening their claim on the place: thinking of leaving, feeling unwelcome, or simply busy. As always, the change is a reason to look more closely, not a conclusion.

Read the objects people leave behind. They are claims written in things.
teach.disconfirm: If personal markers left on tables or seats in public places turned out to keep newcomers away no longer than no markers at all, the marker findings would not hold where you live. Watching a busy café for an hour will usually settle it.

teach.h: Invasion brings flight, and sometimes a fight.
teach.p:
In 1966 Nancy Felipe and Robert Sommer ran a simple and slightly uncomfortable experiment. A researcher sat down right next to people who were sitting alone, on benches in the grounds of a hospital and at large, mostly empty tables in a university library, close enough to invade their space but saying nothing. People who were invaded in this way left much sooner than similar people who were left alone. Many first tried to restore their space by shifting, turning away or building a barrier of books and bags.

Responses to territorial invasion can also be oddly hostile. In 1997 Barry Ruback and Daniel Juieng watched drivers leaving spaces in a shopping-centre car park. Drivers took longer to leave when another car was waiting for their space, and longer still when the waiting driver sounded the horn, even though staying longer served no purpose. People defended a space they were about to give up anyway, against someone who had a perfectly good reason to want it, and few of them would have described what they were doing as defence.

These responses are worth recognising in others and in yourself. The irritation you feel when someone takes your usual seat, the urge to linger in a parking space someone is waiting for, the sharp words over a shared fridge shelf, are territorial responses, and they are usually out of proportion to the material stakes. Knowing that does not make them disappear, but it can stop you from reading them as something more personal than they are.

When a dispute over space seems far more heated than the space deserves, territory is often the reason.
teach.disconfirm: If drivers left parking spaces just as quickly when someone was waiting, or faster, territorial lingering would not be operating in your setting. Try timing a few departures with and without a waiting car, from a discreet distance.
teach.pullQuote: When a dispute over space seems more heated than the space deserves, territory is often the reason.

teach.p:
Sports teams win more often at home, a finding so consistent across sports and decades that researchers treat it as one of the most reliable patterns in the field, though its causes are debated. Something similar happens in ordinary life. In 2011 Graham Brown and Markus Baer set up negotiations in which one party was on their own territory, an office they had been given time to make their own, and the other was a visitor. Negotiators on home ground tended to achieve better outcomes, and the researchers linked the advantage to the greater confidence people felt in their own space.

For a reader, this means that behaviour has to be read against whose territory it is. A man who is quiet and careful in your office may be expansive and funny in his workshop, his kitchen or his club. A child who is shy at school may be bossy at home. A colleague who seems hesitant in head office may be decisive on the shop floor she runs. Each of them is showing a real part of themselves, and neither setting gives you the whole picture.

It also suggests a courtesy. If you want to understand someone, or want them to feel at ease, meet them on their ground or on neutral ground, rather than summoning them to yours. A manager who visits a team member's workspace to talk, rather than calling them to his office, is giving up a little home advantage, and often gets a franker conversation in return.

And when you are the visitor, remember that part of what you feel, the slight awkwardness, the deference to your host's habits, is the territory speaking, not the person.

Before you judge how someone behaves, notice whose ground you are both standing on.
teach.disconfirm: If people you know behaved in just the same way on their own ground, on yours and on neutral ground, territory would not be shaping their behaviour much. Compare one person you know well in two or three settings before deciding.

teach.p:
In 2002 Sam Gosling and colleagues sent observers into the offices and bedrooms of people they had never met, and asked them to rate the occupants' personalities from the rooms alone. The observers agreed with each other strongly, and on some traits they were reasonably accurate when compared with the occupants' own ratings and those of people who knew them. Openness to new experience was the easiest to judge, from the range of books, music and objects. Conscientiousness showed in how organised the space was.

Gosling described two kinds of clue. Identity claims are deliberate statements: posters, photographs, awards, flags, the objects a person chooses to display to say who they are or wish to be. Behavioural residue is what everyday life leaves behind without any intention: the piled papers, the empty mugs, the worn path in a carpet. Both are informative, and they can disagree, which is itself interesting.

Rooms are a powerful source of information, and that is exactly why they need the ethics described in Part VI. A room you are invited into is information shared under the norms of the invitation. A colleague's open office during a meeting is one thing; their drawers are another. Reading a friend's bookshelves while they make tea is ordinary curiosity. Reading their post is not. The chapter on the ethics of reading people calls this contextual integrity: the question is not only what you can see, but where the information was offered and where it may go.

Rooms also mislead. A sparse office may belong to someone who has just moved in, or works mostly elsewhere, or shares the room, or simply keeps their life at home. A cluttered one may belong to someone far more organised than it looks.

Read a room as a person's claims, and remember that claims are not the whole person.
teach.disconfirm: If observers' judgments of people from their rooms turned out to agree neither with each other nor with the occupants, rooms would tell you nothing. The study found strong agreement and some accuracy, which is enough to be useful and not enough to be sure.

teach.p:
Because territory is bound up with identity, losing it can feel like a loss of self. In 2003 Kimberly Elsbach studied employees whose company moved from assigned desks to a system in which nobody had a fixed place. Many described the change as a threat to their sense of who they were at work. Without a desk to personalise, they lost a way of showing their status, their distinctiveness and their place in the team, and some found ways to reclaim it: arriving early to get the same desk every day, carrying their belongings around in boxes, or claiming particular corners as their own.

The same pattern appears far beyond offices. A man who retires loses not only a job but a desk, a parking space, a workshop, a seat in meetings. A family that moves house loses rooms full of history. A parent whose children leave home finds their territory changed. A widower faces the empty side of the bed. A teenager who must share a bedroom with a new step-sibling loses the first space that was theirs alone.

Territorial loss often shows itself indirectly. People become irritable about small encroachments, over-mark the space they still have, guard objects more closely, or withdraw from shared spaces altogether. These behaviours are easy to misread as bad temper or rudeness. Read against a recent loss of territory, they often make immediate sense.

When someone's behaviour around space changes, ask what space they have lost.

And when you are the cause of someone's territorial loss, as a new partner moving in, a manager reorganising an office, a new step-parent, give them some space that is clearly and lastingly theirs. It costs little and it settles a great deal.
teach.disconfirm: If people who had recently lost an important territory, such as a desk, a room or a home, behaved no differently around space than people who had not, the link between territory and identity would be weak. In your own experience, think of one such change and what followed.

teach.h: Read the claims, and respect them.
teach.p:
Bring this together into a few practical habits. When you enter a space, notice its claims: whose desk, whose seat, whose side, whose marker. When behaviour in a space seems puzzling, ask whose territory it is and whether anyone has recently gained or lost some. When a dispute about space is out of proportion to the stakes, consider that it may be about belonging rather than the space itself.

Respect claims, including small ones. Ask before using someone's desk or chair, even when it is technically shared. Knock on a teenager's door and wait. Do not move someone's marker without asking. When someone new joins a household or a team, give them a place that is clearly theirs, a drawer, a shelf, a desk, a peg for their coat, and you will often see them settle faster.

Notice your own claims too. Most people underestimate how much space they take in shared places: the bag on the seat beside them on a busy train, the papers spread across a shared table, the wide stance on a crowded bench, the car that always takes the best space. Others read these claims as clearly as you read theirs, and they form impressions of you from them.

Finally, remember that some people have very little territory of their own: the person sharing a room in a hostel, the patient on a ward, the carer who lives in someone else's house. Small gestures of respect for the scraps of space they do have, knocking, asking, not touching their things, can matter to them a great deal.

Territory is identity with walls. Treat it accordingly.
teach.disconfirm: If respecting people's small territorial claims, by asking and knocking, made no difference to how comfortable they were with you, the advice in this block would add nothing. Try it with one person for a month and ask them afterwards.

poseGallery.doCaption: Taking only your share of it.
poseGallery.annotation: Others read your territorial claims as clearly as you read theirs. Taking more than your share of a shared space is noticed.

poseGallery.doCaption: Knocking, and waiting at the door.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Walking straight into a teenager's room.
poseGallery.annotation: A bedroom is often a young person's first primary territory. Respecting its door respects the person.

poseGallery.doCaption: Choosing a place at a respectful distance.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Sitting right beside the one person on an empty bench.
poseGallery.annotation: Felipe and Sommer found that people invaded in this way left much sooner. Unnecessary closeness in public space is felt as invasion.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Treating a colleague's desk as yours to use.
poseGallery.annotation: Secondary territories are claimed informally but felt strongly. A quick question avoids a surprising amount of resentment.

caseStudy:
Frank, sixty-three, retires after forty years as an engineer. For the first few weeks he enjoys being at home. Then he starts helping in the kitchen. He reorganises the cupboards so that things are where he thinks they should be, rearranges the drawer of utensils, and takes over the Sunday cooking. His wife, Linda, who has run the kitchen for thirty-five years, becomes short with him. They argue about where the colander should live. Frank tells a friend that retirement is putting a strain on the marriage.

His friend asks a question Frank has not considered: what did he lose when he retired? Frank thinks about it. He lost a desk he had sat at for fifteen years, a parking space with his name on it, a workshop where everyone knew which tools were his, and a seat at the end of the Monday meeting. And he has been trying, without realising it, to claim new territory in the one room that was most clearly Linda's.

That evening he asks Linda, carefully, whether he has been taking over the kitchen. She laughs, a little sharply, and says yes, and that she has started to feel like a guest in her own house. They put the cupboards back the way she had them.

Frank clears out the garden shed, which has been full of junk for years, and turns it into a workshop with a bench, a radio and a pegboard for his tools. He joins a volunteer group that repairs bicycles for a local charity, and within a month he has a regular place at the end of their bench too. He still cooks on Sundays, when Linda asks him to, and he asks where things are.

The arguments stop. Linda tells her sister that Frank seems more himself. Frank thinks it is because he has somewhere to be himself in.
observe: In a café, library or train, notice the markers people leave to hold their places, and how newcomers respond to them.
Notice the seats in your home or workplace that are usually taken by the same person, and what happens when someone else sits in one.
Notice your own territorial claims in a shared space today, such as a bag on a seat or papers on a table, and how much space they take.

drills.name: Territory Map
steps: Draw a simple plan of your home or workplace.
Mark each space as primary, secondary or public territory, and for whom.
Note any space whose ownership is unclear or disputed.
Mark any space that has recently changed hands or been lost by someone.
Write one sentence about any tension you have noticed around those spaces.

drills.name: Marker Watch
steps: In a busy café, library or waiting room, watch for personal markers left on tables and seats.
For each, note what the marker was and how long it held the space.
Note how newcomers responded to marked and unmarked places.
Note any time a neighbour defended a marked place.
Write down which kinds of marker seemed strongest.

drills.name: Whose Ground
steps: Choose one person you know well and recall how they behave in two different settings, such as their home and your workplace.
Note differences in their volume, posture, humour and decisiveness.
Consider whose territory each setting was.
Write down which version of them you had been treating as the real one.
Plan one conversation with them on their ground or neutral ground, and note any difference.

drills.name: Room Reading, Ethically
steps: The next time you are invited into someone's home or office, notice what is on display without touching or opening anything.
Separate what you see into identity claims, such as photographs and posters, and behavioural residue, such as clutter and wear.
Afterwards, write two impressions the room gave you.
For each impression, write one ordinary explanation that would make it misleading.
Do not share your impressions with anyone else.

drills.name: Your Claims
steps: For one day, notice every territorial claim you make in shared spaces, such as seats, tables, desks, fridges and parking.
Note how much space each takes, compared with what you need.
Notice whether anyone had to work around one of your claims.
Choose one claim to reduce.
Note whether anyone seems to notice the difference.

quiz.q: Drivers leaving a car-park space are watched by another driver waiting for it. What did Ruback and Juieng find?
options: Drivers left noticeably faster, out of courtesy to the person waiting
Drivers left at exactly the same speed whether anyone was waiting or not
Drivers took longer when someone was waiting, as if defending the space
Drivers left the space only after making eye contact with the waiting driver
quiz.explain: Drivers lingered when someone was waiting, and longer still if honked at. Territorial responses are often out of proportion to the stakes, and people rarely notice them in themselves.

quiz.q: In Irwin Altman's terms, what kind of territory is your regular seat at a local pub?
options: Secondary: used regularly and claimed, but not owned
Primary: owned, exclusive and central to your identity
Public: temporary, and held only while you sit in it
Not territory at all, since nobody owns a seat in a pub
quiz.explain: Secondary territories are claimed informally through regular use. The claim is real and felt strongly, but it is negotiable, which is why disputes over them are so common.

quiz.q: What did Gosling and colleagues find when strangers judged people's personalities from their offices and bedrooms?
options: They could judge nothing at all beyond how tidy each room was
They were wrong about every trait they were asked to judge
They judged accurately only when shown photos of the occupant
They agreed strongly, and judged some traits fairly accurately
quiz.explain: Observers agreed with each other and were reasonably accurate on some traits, especially openness. Rooms carry real information, which is why reading them needs the ethics of where that information was offered.

quiz.q: Your teenage son has started keeping his bedroom door closed and objects when you walk in without knocking. What fits this chapter?
options: Insist on an open door, since a closed one means he is hiding something
Treat it as an ordinary claim on his territory; knock and wait
Take the door off its hinges until he explains what is going on
Search the room while he is out to make sure nothing is wrong
quiz.explain: A bedroom is often a young person's first primary territory, and claiming it is ordinary. Respecting the door respects him; real concerns about safety are a reason to talk with him, not to invade the space.

quiz.q: In Felipe and Sommer's study, what happened when a researcher sat right beside people sitting alone on benches and at library tables?
options: They moved closer to the researcher and began conversations
They took no notice and stayed for the same length of time
They left much sooner than people who were not approached
They asked the researcher to move, politely, in almost every case
quiz.explain: Invaded people first tried to restore their space by shifting, turning or building barriers, and then left. Unnecessary closeness in a public place is felt as invasion even without a word.

quiz.q: After your office moves to hot-desking, a usually easy-going colleague turns irritable and arrives early every day to claim the same desk. What fits?
options: Losing his own desk may feel like a threat to his identity; he is reclaiming one
He is being selfish and should be told to use a different desk each day
He is unhappy with the company and is probably planning to leave soon
He is anxious about something at home and needs the routine to cope
quiz.explain: Studies of desk-sharing found many people experienced losing a fixed place as a threat to who they were at work, and reclaimed space in just this way. Read against a territorial loss, his behaviour makes sense.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific territory that matters to you, a seat, a desk, a room, a side of the bed, a place at a table. How would you feel if someone else began using it without asking? Then think of a time when you gained or lost a territory, by moving house, changing jobs, retiring or someone new joining your household. How did your behaviour around space change afterwards? What did the people around you make of it?
reflection.guidance: Most people are surprised by how strongly they feel about a space they do not even own. The second part is often where the insight lies: behaviour that looked like bad temper to others may have been a response to a territorial loss that nobody named. Naming it, to yourself and to the people affected, is often enough to ease it.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to miss territory altogether and read territorial behaviour as personality: the colleague who guards his desk as possessive, the parent who snaps about the kitchen as irritable, the teenager who closes his door as secretive. The second is to ignore other people's claims, sitting in the regular seat, using the shared desk without asking, moving someone's things, and then being surprised by the reaction. The third is to read rooms without ethics, treating anything visible as yours to examine and discuss. And the fourth is to forget your own claims, taking more than your share of shared space while resenting others who do the same. Ask whose space it is, respect small claims, and remember that territory is identity with walls.

watch.title: Don't Mess With Sheldon's Spot!
watch.notice: A comic compilation built on one man's claim to a single seat on a sofa. Exaggerated, but recognisable: notice how the others work around claimed territory, and what happens when it is taken.
